item.description:
Back in July, new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced a total of 3,200 job cuts across Microsoft's gaming arm, with roughly half of those cuts being made alongside that announcement. The impact was vast. Various developers at Xbox studios, including Activision, Bethesda, Id Software, Blizzard, Mojang, and King suffered layoffs. Double Fine and Compulsion were thrust into independence, while Dishonored 2's Arkane Lyon, State of Decay 3's Undead Labs, and Hellblade's Ninja Theory entered terms for new ownership.
Then, two weeks ago, Xbox made more sweeping cuts. Halo Studios has been drastically reduced in size, with Activision taking control of the sci-fi franchise. Rare and World's Edge were shunted under Activision's umbrella, with the Age of Empires studio reportedly losing roughly half its developers in the process. Obsidian was absorbed by Bethesda, and Ninja Theory entered a consultation process in preparation for a potential closure as its new ownership deal fell through. Undead Labs suffered heavy layoffs as it went independent, while Arkane Lyon is still in a period of consultation with its staff. At least 268 more roles were eliminated in total in that latest round, though it's unclear whether these also include the developers at the likes of Ninja Theory and Undead Labs.
But there's been one Xbox-owned studio left largely off the cutting block so far: Gears of War: E-Day developer The Coalition. Now, following the latest wave of Microsoft cuts - including the sudden departure of E-Day's story director, Juan Vaca - Eurogamer has learned staff at the studio have become increasingly fearful of imminent layoffs, and the potentially major financial consequences which could follow. Eurogamer spoke to multiple sources at the Vancouver-based studio with knowledge of the situation for this article, who have been provided anonymity to protect their identity.
It's worth noting that this sense of trepidation wasn't always the case. Before the latest round of Xbox layoffs, developers at The Coalition had been cautiously optimistic. They believed The Coalition had been spared the cuts, at least thus far, for two main reasons: first, they were working on a big, imminent release for Xbox, in the upcoming Gears of War: E-Day - laying off developers still working on a game would make little sense.
Second, the studio maintains a status as one of Xbox's "good children, so to speak", as one source put it to Eurogamer. The studio's official site, for instance, describes it as "a flagship first-party studio within Xbox Game Studios" and the "home to one of gaming's most critically and commercially acclaimed series" in the long-running Gears of War. Xbox leadership, meanwhile, has largely had a "hands-off" approach to managing the studio over the years, which was, at least for The Coalition, a situation that had seemingly been working well. Those two factors combined to create a sense of relative safety.
Naturally, the knowledge that Xbox still had many job cuts to go still had an impact on morale. Prior gut-punches, such as Tango Gameworks' shock closure after the release of the critically-acclaimed Hi-Fi Rush, were "still on everybody's minds", as one source put it to Eurogamer back in July, shortly after the first stage of Xbox's self-described reset. But the belief continued that it simply wouldn't be smart to "cannibalise" the studio.
Another source had similarly mixed feelings at the time. They felt Microsoft had "faith" in The Coalition, following years of positive support, and that development of Gears of War: E-Day itself was in a good place. But they too felt uneasy, following the first 1,600 job cuts and massive restructuring, describing the mood as "cautious", with the remaining, unspecified layoffs of the 3,200 said to be "hanging over our heads." Energy at the studio was "not full death-march", but at least muted, as they put it, and would likely remain so until three-months after E-Day's release. "The mood is certainly 'let's not celebrate the game until we're three months post launch, just in case', which is very unusual," they said.
Notably, this same source claimed the team had been "crunching hard" in the final months before E-Day's launch, but even then, at the time the atmosphere still wasn't overtly negative. This strenuous push towards the finish line by E-Day developers, for instance, was rewarded with extra vacation time. While the amount given varied from person to person, gestures such as these - despite the crunch - were cited as helping to alleviate worries among staff. Regarding the practice of crunch itself at the studio, Eurogamer understands the internal position is that "extra work" is viewed as occasionally necessary for games such as this, and there is an acknowledgement the team has been working "incredibly hard" on E-Day. The issue of crunch remains a major issue in game development, despite much reporting on the matter and promises of changed culture at various studios over the years.
Ultimately, combined with The Coalition having been largely sheltered from Microsoft's cuts at the time, the sense earlier this summer was that Xbox was "invested" in long-term support in the studio. Cautious optimism remained the ruling sentiment.
That feeling had persisted - until this month. Last week, Gears of War: E-Day's story director Juan Vaca announced he had been laid off as part of Microsoft's cuts, barely two weeks before the game's release. At that time it was unclear how many other developers had been cut. A source speaking to Kotaku claimed a "handful" of developers were also laid off from the studio, shortly before Vaca, for reasons separate from the wider Xbox layoffs. Multiple sources have also told Eurogamer that staff were quietly let go at The Coalition in the past few weeks.
Their departure, along with Vaca's, has taken a hammer to the remaining optimism at the studio. One source described Vaca's departure as "very demoralising". As they put it: "I can only imagine the heartbreak of spending all those years on a game to have the final stretch ripped away, completely out of your control. It's like you planned for a year on a meal for your family where everyone will be there and the day of, you get locked out of the building or something and can't join in."
Coalition developers as a result are "unhappy about it and on edge", they added, "because we honestly expected the layoffs to hit us post-release, but that seems to not matter now. Now we're just expecting the next wave, or being reorganised under Activision or something later this year."
Beyond the stress, meanwhile, Vaca and others' departures have also raised concerns of a financial nature: staff are now concerned that, were they to be laid off within a few weeks of Gears of War: E-Day's release as some fear, they may miss out on potentially lucrative Metacritic bonuses.
The existence of this bonus scheme itself isn't irregular; Metacritic bonuses tied to a game's critical reception have been an established practice at game development studios for years. Likewise the stipulations involved are standard. An internal email, verified by Eurogamer, confirms the existence of this bonus and its relatively typical nature.
However, given the threat of ongoing Xbox cuts, one aspect of this Metacritic bonus has become a cause for concern. In order to be eligible to receive the bonus, developers must be full-time employees at the time of the payout. Studio leadership have communicated to The Coalition developers that this payout date "should be near the end of October", as one source put it.
As a result, it has been unclear to developers still at the studio and who have recently left whether those such as Juan Vaca, who were recently laid off by Xbox and therefore are no longer employed at The Coalition - but will technically still be on payroll at the time of the payout in late October - will receive this bonus if the game hits its targets. Eurogamer understands that despite concerns, those recently impacted, such as Vaca, will still receive their bonuses if the targets are met.
What remains uncertain, however - and crucially so for developers at The Coalition today - is the question of what happens to current staff's bonuses if they are laid off immediately following the release of Gears of War: E-Day as some now fear. As of now, it is still unclear whether these developers would receive their Metacritic bonus.
As a result, a source told Eurogamer that developers being laid off before the Metacritic bonus payout has now become a "morbid joke" among members of the team. The assumption among them, for instance, had been that Vaca would not be receiving his bonus, which could account for tens of thousands of dollars. The possibility of layoffs before the bonus payout has become the "biggest concern" among staff.
Multiple sources have told Eurogamer that the wider actions of Microsoft, in laying off large numbers of staff and cutting multiple studios, has also manifested in a significant amount of scepticism, with some at The Coalition expecting an attempt to "avoid" paying out Metacritic bonuses to any developers hypothetically laid off just before or right after E-Day's release.
Another source said that while those potentially laid off shortly before the payout should technically be eligible for the bonus, they still remained doubtful: "It's hard to believe anything [Microsoft leadership] say anymore after discarding staff in this manner," they explained. Another expressed similar scepticism, saying they "wouldn't put it past Microsoft" to try and avoid paying these bonuses out to any potentially laid off employees.
One more put it like this: "There was a general perception here that we're in a relatively secure spot, despite everything in the industry. But now that feeling is up in the air."
All in all, Xbox's "reset" has, in a matter of months, taken the morale of a strong studio, on the eve of an exciting triple-A release, and turned it sour. With continued cuts planned across Xbox, estimated to still be in the many hundreds at least, time will soon tell whether these fears are unfounded, or if what should be a celebratory milestone for The Colition's developers is spoiled by decisions made far above their heads.

Ubisoft also revealed Massive's work on a brand new, original game called March of Giants. Read more
item.description:
Ubisoft has expanded the remit of Swedish studio Massive Entertainment - responsible for The Division series, Star Wars Outlaws and Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora - to become a second major part of the company and include more of its studios and game brands. Ubisoft also revealed Massive's work on a brand new, original game called March of Giants.
Ubisoft's Creative House 2 cluster of studios now joins the expanded Massive Entertainment brand, the company announced this week, which means Massive Entertainment now governs the Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon and Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell brands, and multiple studios around the world.
"The Massive Entertainment brand builds on a nearly three-decade legacy established in Sweden through its games and technology, earning the trust of players and recognition from industry peers alike," Massive said in a press release.
Christoph Hartmann, who was appointed as general manager of Ubisoft Creative House 2 earlier this year, has become general manager of Massive Entertainment amidst the reorganisation. "Bringing our teams together under one identity gives us the opportunity to combine the creative energy and expertise across Montréal, Paris, Sweden and Toronto to shape the next generation of these iconic franchises, create new games and IPs, and push our craft and technology forward," he said.
Nothing further was revealed about March of Giants, other than its name, and that it's an original game idea.
This is another step in Ubisoft's ongoing restructuring, which previously saw the publisher form a new subsidiary company called Vantage Studios - following a €1.16bn Tencent investment - to oversee its biggest gaming brands: Assassin's Creed, Far Cry and Rainbow Six. This new move establishes Massive Entertainment as the other multi-franchise-leading subsidiary within Ubisoft.
As a result of this reorganisation, Ubisoft has undergone several rounds of layoffs. In January, the company closed its Halifax and Stockholm studios and laid off staff at Ubisoft Abu Dhabi, Redlynx, and even Massive Entertainment itself. In March, Ubisoft reportedly let go of 105 staff at Ghost Recon studio Red Storm Entertainment, relegating it to a support studio. And in June, Ubisoft reportedly shuttered its Winnipeg and Belgrade studios, and removed staff at Ubisoft Barcelona - amounting to 380 layoffs.

item.title: Halo's ex-franchise director, Frank O'Connor, has given Activision a few pointers now that it's in charge of making the next Halo game with a "purpose-built team." Top of the list, hire some devs who were laid off from Bungie and Halo Studios. Read more
item.description:
Halo's ex-franchise director, Frank O'Connor, has given Activision a few pointers now that it's in charge of making the next Halo game with a "purpose-built team." Top of the list, hire some devs who were laid off from Bungie and Halo Studios.
O'Connor's time with the iconic sci-fi series stretches back to the early 2000s, when he jumped aboard at Bungie and eventually became the series' development director at 343 Industries. He left the studio during an internal shakeup in 2023, shortly before 343 rebranded into Halo Studios, which has since been gutted due to Xbox's "reset."
His first suggestion is that Activision could make a "classic" Halo game with the series' familiar, heavy movement and chaotic sandbox "tailored to a core audience [and] scaled" to also be "attractive to a broader one so it can grow (not to mention [the] obvious fact that Halo MP is better [with] more people playing, by mathematical default)."
Activision's second path, according to O'Connor, sounds like a completely modernised and substantially different Halo - one that "reinvents the game/universe in a surprising but fantastic way." What that would look like is anyone's guess. "Maybe it's a new take on the FPS, maybe it's an action RPG," O'Connor wrote. Either way, it would get "a small head start based on curiosity or loyalty." The idea of a full-on lore reboot wasn't totally popular with series fans.
And, finally, there's the third path, which basically sounds like Call of Halo. O'Connor said the company could "translate Halo IP and sandbox into the [Activision] comfort zone," by using the "player progress and business models that are proven to work" time and again in the Call of Duty series. Activision could then "craft a big annual or semi-annual spectacle and constant content," much like it does for its other heavyweight military shooter.
The ex-Halo boss then ended with two more bonus tips. One, "Hire Bungie, Halo Studios and other laid off folk who are bursting with talent and ideas that got nerfed or shut down over the years." The second is to avoid tying the next Halo to "hardware/service launch cycles" or forcing it to launch on aging platforms - like Halo Infinite's Xbox One version.
Activision's Halo is still likely years away since the publisher hasn't even assembled a new team for the project yet. Here's hoping Master Chief's next comeback isn't as bumpy as his last - checks notes - four attempts.

item.title: Despite mass layoffs at multiple first-party studios and major internal shakeups, CEO Asha Sharma has shot down speculation about a potential Xbox buyout. Read more
item.description:
Despite mass layoffs at multiple first-party studios and major internal shakeups, CEO Asha Sharma has shot down speculation about a potential Xbox buyout.
This year, Xbox began a corporate "reset" that plans to cut a total of 3,200 jobs across the company before next summer. So far, the restructure has resulted in three studios going independent (Double Fine, Compulsion Games, Undead Labs), while the fate of Hellblade maker Ninja Theory and Dishonored studio Arkane remains up in the air.
In another dramatic turn earlier this month, Xbox handed Activision the keys to the entire Halo series. Rare and World's Edge (of Age of Empires fame) also moved under the Call of Duty publisher, while Obsidian Entertainment got slotted into Bethesda. That leaves only a handful of developers under the Xbox Game Studios umbrella - The Coalition (Gears of War), Playground Games (Fable, Forza), Mojang (Minecraft), InXile Entertainment (Clockwork Revolution) and what's left of Halo Studios.
To many, this looked like an attempt at streamlining the business to make it more attractive for potential buyers. (Microsoft might have struggled to sell Rare by itself, for example, but that becomes a much easier task when it's bundled in with the company in control of Call of Duty.) A sale isn't on the table at all, however, according to Sharma.
Speaking to The New York Times, she put it plainly: "Xbox is not for sale… We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that."
As NYT noted, Sharma's answer doesn't completely rule out the possibility of Xbox being spun off as an independent entity that still works closely with Microsoft, like some analysts have suggested. There's no signs of that so far, at least.
"We've got a long way to go with Microsoft," Sharma added, “and we're going to take the long-term view."
From here, the console maker is hoping next week's Gears of War: E-Day and next year's Clockwork Revolution can still make a splash as Xbox console exclusives. Sharma also recently signed a deal with Kojima Productions on its action-stealth game Physint, after rival PlayStation pulled funding from the project.

item.title: If you thought Red Dead Redemption 2's heavy winds and even heavier rain looked impressive, you might be happy to learn that Rockstar Games went back and "re-engineered our weather system" for GTA 6. Hurricanes, rainbows and "vertiginous cumulonimbus clouds" are all part of the upcoming open worlder. Read more
item.description:
If you thought Red Dead Redemption 2's heavy winds and even heavier rain looked impressive, you might be happy to learn that Rockstar Games went back and "re-engineered our weather system" for GTA 6. Hurricanes, rainbows and "vertiginous cumulonimbus clouds" are all part of the upcoming open worlder.
That's according to the studio's vice president of art for lighting and rendering, Owen Shepherd, who spoke to Game Informer about Grand Theft Auto 6's supposedly much-improved tech.
"We have re-engineered our weather system to make everything much more localized and persistent, and really wanted the world to feel dynamically solid and achieve a sense of scale we haven't felt before," Shepherd told the magazine. "The world features new fully dynamic cloudscapes that roll across the map, these give us a broad spectrum of weather from the clear blue skies of a Miami winter to the vertiginous cumulonimbus clouds with sporadic lightning that you see most afternoons in the Floridian summer and autumn."
The "localized and persistent" weather is particularly interesting. You can apparently take a break from robbing shops and doomscrolling through in-game social media apps to witness a rain shower pouring over a totally different area - all while you're as dry as a crunchy autumn leaf. The after effects of that faraway storm (rainbows and wet pavements and puddles) will stay well after it's subsided, as well.
All cool details, but I suspect we're all curious about what those hurricanes and thunderstorms actually look like. Rockstar isn't giving much away for now, though Shepherd did describe the intended effect. "Heavy clouds, strong winds, dense atmospherics, and a lot of rain combine so that everything is dripping wet, water is gushing off roof edges and lampposts, thunder rumbles and flashes of lightning light up the clouds dramatically," he said.
Rockstar's also omitting how these updated weather systems might impact how you move around the world. Are thunderstorms purely aesthetic or will the wet roads affect my tires? What happens if I fly a plane into a hurricane or parachute during Leonida's windier days? I suspect the answer is that I'll end up 'Wasted' before long. GTA 6 comes to PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November, so there's not long left until we can find out for ourselves.
Elsewhere in the Game Informer spotlight, the studio confirmed there's over 170 animal species in the world, including 60 different birds and more than 30 land mammals. Underwater scuba-diving is also back, so expect manatees and jellyfish and whales. GTA 6 is borrowing another Red Dead Redemption 2 feature, as well, in the form of discoverable animals you can study and Legendary animals the studio's still keeping a lid on.

item.title: Valve's new MOBA Deadlock - a sort of cross between Dota and Overwatch - might not be fully released yet, or even accessible by vast portions of the public,but that hasn't stopped its latest update propelling it to being one of the most played games on Steam. Read more
item.description:
Valve's new MOBA Deadlock - a sort of cross between Dota and Overwatch - might not be fully released yet, or even accessible by vast portions of the public,but that hasn't stopped its latest update propelling it to being one of the most played games on Steam.
Yesterday, Valve released a huge City Never Sleeps update for Deadlock. This drastically overhauled the map, added six new heroes, introduced a deluge of fresh voice lines, and included multiple HUD and quality-of-life updates. It was a major moment for the game, which is still yet to get a release date.
Even so, those who do have access to Deadlock flew to it in droves. The game quickly climbed the rankings in Steam's most played category, and yesterday it reached 228,086 concurrent players,according to SteamDB - the largest figure in its history.
Among the many additions the Deadlock community has attached itself to in the City Never Sleeps update are the new voice lines. The update more than doubled the character interaction lines. The Deadlock Reddit page is full of highlights picked out by players, who are delighted to see more personality expressed by the game's growing cast of oddball characters.
Another highlight is the visual update to Deadlock's New York-inspired map: The Cursed Apple. Different segments are now themed distinctly, so the central blue lane is Broadway, the green lane is Greenwich, and the yellow lane is York. Between each lane are smaller districts such as the Theatre, Chinatown, the Haunted Lot, and the Plaza. Each lane and district have unique Haunts (PvE enemies) that fit the new look too. It's impressive stuff you can see for yourself on the Deadlock website.
As Deadlock continues to pick up steam (on Steam), you've got to wonder just how big this game can get as it inevitably chugs along to a full release. If you want to play Deadlock, you'll have to find someone with access who can gift you an invite code. Get socialising!

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever players claim to have been sent a survey asking whether they'd be interested in a variety of new classes for the upcoming MMO - and some of them are very interesting. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever players claim to have been sent a survey asking whether they'd be interested in a variety of new classes for the upcoming MMO - and some of them are very interesting.
Over the past few days, a select few users of Blizzard's Battle.net launcher spotted an opt-in survey. While Blizzard requested participants not share details of this survey, screenshots and information have nevertheless leaked online. As a result, popular World of Warcraft YouTubers such as Belluar have covered its contents.
Eurogamer cannot verify the accuracy of the survey information out in the wild, but if what's out there is accurate, it hints towards some intriguing new World of Warcraft class ideas. According to users on the Classic WoW Reddit, the surveyed classes are:
The classes that appear to have been polled in this survey can be split between wholly new ideas, or spins on established classes from modern World of Warcraft. Some examples of those refreshed classes include Death Knights, Demon Hunters, and Monks. But these would likely have significantly different playstyles given the significant differences between modern WoW and WoW: Forever.
For example, per alleged survey information on the Demon Hunter, the class would be far slower and less mobile than its World of Warcraft: Legion counterpart. Likewise, these demon hunters would not be members of Illidan's faction of demon hunters we've grown to love; rather a smaller pre-existing faction out somewhere in Azeroth, separate from his shirtless edginess.
As for those newer class ideas, there are some real winners here. The Tinker is one such example, with roots in the Warcraft RTS series from yesteryear. Per the survey details leaked online, the Tinker pilots a mech suit to fit your playstyle, able to tank hits, unleash big damage, or act in a supporting role. Also, this proposed class would have two lives: the mech and the pilot within (a bit like D.Va in Overwatch). Alternatively you have the San'layn, which are vampiric knights in full plate armour, who suck the vitality from foes and excel in melee combat.
Whether Blizzard actually ends up implementing any or all of these remains to be seen, but this would mark a major new avenue of expanding the Classic World of Warcraft setting without venturing back into expansions like The Burning Crusade or Wrath of the Lich King. Of these classes, which would you like to see added? If you've not had a chance to play World of Warcraft: Forever's beta yet, Eurogamer's early impressions from the 1-20 levelling journey were glowing.

item.title: Yesterday's free Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered upgrade might have propelled the old role-playing game to new heights, in terms of player popularity, but not everyone is happy with what's changed. A particular point of contention concerns the game's new lighting changes, which some people think has made The Witcher 3 too bright and washed out - though this is not the only issue. Read more
item.description:
Yesterday's free Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered upgrade might have propelled the old role-playing game to new heights, in terms of player popularity, but not everyone is happy with what's changed. A particular point of contention concerns the game's new lighting changes, which some people think has made The Witcher 3 too bright and washed out - though this is not the only issue.
The lighting is such an issue for some people they're asking developer CD Projekt Red for a way to roll back their version of The Witcher 3 - which you can't easily do on console as far as I'm aware (though there are various options on PC). "You people should figure out a way for Xbox users to play the older version because my god this new lighting is lifeless," wrote one irate person on X. "What's the point of removing all whimsy of a fantasy game? Realism is the death of escapism."
"I prefer the old look," said another player on Reddit, who provided detailed comparison images. "It has better contrast, with stronger highlights and a more pronounced overall image." Another video was linked that painstakingly compares the Witcher 3 Remastered edition with the next-gen edition and the original edition of the game.
Exactly what's going on regarding lighting is tricky to pin down, because the changes have occurred for numerous reasons, however the overall issue is notable in comparison screenshots. The Witcher 3 - Remastered does look brighter and seems to have less contrast, and the chief offender seems to be a Bloom setting you can simply turn off on PC, though there's no such option on console, which is another thing aggravating players there.
Exacerbating this are the Remastered edition's new Path Tracing option, for those with computers that can handle it, which does seem to generally brighten areas. But the computing cost is so high, and the changes so negligible, even people with beefy PCs are broadly not in favour of it. The game also appears to have updated HDR settings, making The Witcher 3 blindingly bright for people with screens that can use it.
There are more technical issues besides. PC players with AMD-based systems are reporting a wide array of graphical glitches; Switch 2 owners are reporting blurry visuals when playing the game in handheld mode, even with blur-related graphical options turned off; and the game's audio mix seems off with voices suddenly quiet and music loud, though apparently meditating in game, of all things, fixes this.
Console players on older Xbox Series S hardware are also bemoaning a drop in performance because of this update, which has brought the base minimum specs of the game up, meaning that whereas the game used to run with a high frame-rate, it now does not. And because the update is automatically applied on consoles, there's little they can do about it.
Clearly, many of these issues are bugs and will be fixed, but a bigger question surrounds the broader approach to brightening the game and how intentional this was - in other words: will CD Projekt Red do anything to change it? It's an issue I've contacted the company trying to explore.
However, it's worth mentioning that while many people aren't happy with the game's updated new look, plenty of people are. There are easily as many posts from people stating that the game "looks so much better now", if not more, than posts saying otherwise.
My own experience of The Witcher 3 - Remastered was very positive on PC, though I've not yet had a chance to test it on consoles. Across the game, the changes have made The Witcher 3 feel modern and revitalised, though they don't fundamentally alter what's there.

item.description:
This probably feels like a bit of an odd place to start, but Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons isn't Fable. Yet, when I sat down to watch developer Invoke Studios' Gamescom demo of Warlock with no real idea of what to expect, it was the first thing that popped into my mind. Not because of its striking fantasy landscape - crooked hovels huddled awkwardly amid a vast sprawl of ragged coastline, jagged mountains, and, in the distance, an imposing tower looming over all - but rather the moment early on when Warlock's warrior protagonist Kaatri enters the town of Crickshank and is immediately welcomed with a couple of fruity insults from the locals.
Admittedly, "Well, well, look what the mists dragged in", isn't quite as spirited a greeting as "Arseface". But I couldn't help wondering if Darkon - Warlock's setting, and an area of Dungeons & Dragons' Ravenloft that's slowly being devoured by fog - was aiming to be a similarly reactive sort of sandbox to Fable's Albion. The answer, it turns out, is not quite. Rather, as Invoke general manager Dominique Guay tells me, Warlock's open world is reactive in its own way. The goal here isn't to "create a world that's living without you completely", but the team still wants to make it feel alive. Guay points to the end of Warlock's Gamescom demo as an example, where Kaatri stumbles upon an already unfolding skirmish and can - if a player decides to - join in.
For Invoke, though, the real goal is to put Kaatri's magic - which she acquires after making a pact with her patron, the witch Tasha, in effort to find someone she's lost - at the heart of it all. "Our main focus is first that the world be reactive to your spells and magic," explains Guay. "That's the baseline we're interested in. We were really drawn to magic as a way of expression, as a way of being creative as a player." Magic is such an integral part of Invoke's vision for Warlock, in fact, that it's the first thing the studio shows off in its Gamescom gameplay demo, even before offering a wider look at the world.
Early on, Kaatri is seen wielding her borrowed magic to navigate some brambles blocking her path. She could simply smash through them with her sword, but instead we see her using a cantrip known as Tasha's Leash to snare a nearby lantern and hurl it at the prickly undergrowth, causing it to erupt into flames. Using Tasha's Leash on the resulting inferno would pluck a makeshift fireball into being, but instead, we see her grab some water from a nearby pond and use the shimmering aquatic bauble to douse the flames. This leaves behind a pool of oil that can be similarly commanded - perhaps to throw at enemies, which can be ignited in turn.
It's a simple display of Warlock's magic loop, and as the demo continues, there are hints of how Invoke intends to build on this foundation as play goes on. Down in Crickshank's fog-gripped depths, for instance, we see how Tasha's Leash can interact with a second spell, Black Tentacles. Alone it has basic combat utility, but Kaatri can also conjure a grasping tendril then use Tasha's Leash to yank masonry off the walls. Combining the two creates an impromptu platform she can use to safely cross the deadly miasma.
But there's plenty more in Kaatri's magical arsenal. Misty Step allows her to adopt a non-corporeal form and wispily teleport through grates or around monsters. Eldritch Blast, meanwhile, can obliterate objects and enemies from a distance. More elementally minded players can use wind to push targets, summon rain, or conjure lightning. And in another example of Warlock's synergistic loop, the latter's potency and reach is improved when used in the vicinity of conductive material such as, yes, water. "We didn't want just 'this spell does 10 damage, this spell does 100 damage in this size in that area'," Guay explains. "We want players to be able to improvise, to learn, to be creative with these spells, and so we started from there." In fact, many of the spells are "optional", only found by thoroughly exploring the world.
Warlock isn't solely a game about magic, however, and Kaatri's warrior roots means she's adept at melee combat too. Players are able to equip two weapons at once, in a primary and secondary configuration, with Guay pointing to the likes of swords and warhammers; some single-handed, others requiring two. Weapons, like magic, are upgradable, and the goal here is to give players rich customisation options that continue across armour, gear, enchantments, talismans, and more - the emphasis being on bespoke pieces with their own traits and looks, rather than, as Guay puts it, "just like stats and numbers."
As for the combat rhythm this split between magic and melee creates, Guay explains: "The reality is kind of a dance where you go to spells, you set things up, you go into melee ... then back and forth, [and this] flows well because the spells are directly accessible in the controller." All this together gives Warlock an intriguing foundation, and could provide a distinctive flavour to its action as Kaatri prowls the open-world.
And, honestly, it's the world I'm perhaps most curious about. For the D&D fans out there (if I'm honest, I barely know the difference between a cantrip and a cantaloupe), Invoke is promising plenty of connective tissue, from a tone that fits the "darker, more mature side" of D&D's Domains of Dread universe, to familiar spells and enemies. But perhaps more interesting is the team's pedigree: Guay and others at Invoke are Ubisoft veterans, and - having worked on the likes of Far Cry and Watch Dogs
As Guay puts it, Invoke is keen for players to be the driving force behind their own adventure. "We wanted to really make the game, first and foremost, about exploring a world instead of just following a waypoint around," he says. "We want the player to truly go out there, visit places, be curious, uncover secrets." To that end, Darkon is "pretty large", albeit certainly nothing like - to use Guay's example - Crimson Desert's world. Going too big, he argues, would be a "disservice" to Warlock's focus on exploration.
"We don't want you to have to travel for 15 minutes to find a new location," Guay elaborates. "We want you to be always within like a minute, a minute and a half, of another cool place." Density and diversity appear to be the watchwords here, with Invoke wanting to create "different and crazy environments" while still having the space to transition between them naturally. "It's smaller than those huge worlds," Guay says, "but it feels like an open world. You can get lost in it." And even here, it all comes back to magic.
"We're not making a Metroidvania game," Guay continues, "but to a degree, you'll want to acquire more spells to reach more places. It's not binary like a Metroidvania would be, but there's an element of that in … your ability to traverse terrain and reach new places, [and in] the monsters and the challenges you're gonna have to deal with."
Kaatri's "grim personal quest" might form the backbone of Warlock's structure but Guay says there are "multiple ways" to approach the points that make up her story, "so it's going to flow depending on how you explore the world. That forced us to accept that a lot of our content was optional, and we're okay with that ... we're trying to make sure [we don't] force you down a very narrow critical path." And, crucially, the route forward isn't necessarily an explicit one.
Invoke's aim, says Guay, is to create a "cohesive" world, and as the fog of war slowly lifts through exploration, players can expect to uncover the likes of dungeons, mines (useful for acquiring iron ore for upgrades), and settlements, each with their own "specific, unique mood". However, "it's not like there's an exclamation point [on the map]," notes Guay. "You'll have hints on what you should work on next or how you can further your main quest, but ... you're going to have to listen to people, ask questions, investigate.
"We want to have stories happening in the world instead of us telling you a story," he continues. "Most of our content is just there in the world ... You'll find a cool-looking location, you'll explore it ... and you're like, 'What is this, what happened here, what's going on?' ... And as you do, you'll stumble on side quests which have multiple entry points ... Maybe you'll find a poster or talk to someone [and] you can decide to opt in or out."
Embarking on these stories might involve more combat, but magic also resurfaces as a tool for "open-ended" puzzle-solving. "We want you to be creative with your magic," Guay says, "so it can't be just one solution to a thing." And while side quests are intended to accentuate the narrative, exploration also provides a throughline of steadily increasing power: "Finding new spells, finding raw magic that allows you to upgrade [them], finding rare artefacts, gears. So the kind of adventures you'd expect to do in Dungeons & Dragons."
Invoke is, though, also keen to manage expectations around what it isn't trying to do. Despite coming on the heels of Baldur's Gate 3, Warlock isn't intended to be a game where you can shape Kaatri's story through the likes of conversation trees and dialogue choices. "We're being very clear on that," explains Guay. "Kaatri is a written character, so it's not like you can play evil or good Kaatri. Nothing like that. The main narrative moments you're going to go through are written down, and you're going to go through the same moment as someone else." And you shouldn't expect to be accompanied by a ragtag adventuring party, either.
Although there are "definitely allies you'll make along the way, kind of her found family", the moment-to-moment focus is on Kaatri and her imp companion Skev - a character who can also be spotted in Warlock's Gamescom demo. Skev has gameplay purposes during the adventure - his upgradable skills including lockpicking and distracting enemies during combat - but he's not just a sidekick; he's also intended to be "his own character with his own motivation." As the imp advisor to the disappeared ruler of Darkon, Skev, like Kaatri, is looking for someone. "So there's an ongoing story there of how their relationship grows."
And that is pretty much everything Invoke is saying about Warlock right now. In many ways, it's a familiar proposition with its sprawling dark fantasy open-world, but - having walked into its demo with no foreknowledge, no expectations, and, yes, a fairly minimal understanding of D&D - I walked away impressed with what Invoke is trying to achieve. Of course it's not Fable, but Warlock's own take on reactivity - the focus on synergistic magic that permeates everything from combat to puzzle-solving - is an intriguing one. And I'm curious to see how far Invoke can push it, and how fresh it feels, when Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons launches next year.

item.title: Control Resonant is one of the few modern open-world games which doesn't always point you to where you should go next. This desire to give players time to figure their way around is the reason why, according to the game's director, Resonant does not have yellow paint. Read more
item.description:
Control Resonant is one of the few modern open-world games which doesn't always point you to where you should go next. This desire to give players time to figure their way around is the reason why, according to the game's director, Resonant does not have yellow paint.
"It was a conscious decision, obviously," Control Resonant director Mikael Kasurinen said on the Dropped Frames podcast (via Kotaku). Kasurinen went on to explain he believes player autonomy is one of the key factors that make a good game.
"It's not like the game is telling me what to do and I just go and do it. I feel like I'm the one making the decisions in the game," he added. "It's so important that the players feel like they're the ones figuring it out."
Yellow / white paint has become the subject of ridicule in recent years. By covering ledges, climbable walls and other surfaces with said paint, games - especially open-world - attempt to grab the player's attention to point them in the right direction and ensure they don't get lost.
However, excessive use of yellow paint is something players have been increasingly rejecting. Things seemingly came to a head with Marvel's Wolverine, another triple-A game released right around the same time as Resonant. Players dubbed the game's blue scent trails, which act as a constant reminder of where you should go next, as "fart trails".
Developer Insomniac Games eventually added a toggle to turn it off in most situations, but the damage had already been done. On top of the visible markers, Wolverine also has white paint to signify ledges that boost the player's jump, as well as walls the player can climb.
Remedy's decision not to rely on similar tricks is especially notable given the larger size of Resonant's map compared to the original Control, which took place inside an office building and relied mostly on diegetic signs in the world to orient players.
Now, Resonant does utilise the colour yellow with certain objects in the world, but because of the industrial design of many of those surfaces, it looks far more organic, like something you'd see if you visited a shipping yard or factory floor.
Kasurinen indicated he's not entirely against the practice, it only has to fit thematically within the game's world, saying, "You have to find the right balance between 'here's the world' and 'here are the different themes and elements that you have to pay attention to.' But it has to feel like it's on you to make a decision on what to do with those elements that you see within the world.
"If it feels like, 'go here,' it's not anymore a decision for the player. Somebody has already decided for you."
Many have called on developers to afford players a bit more trust, and for a return to the days of games relying on framing, lighting and other visual aides to guide players around levels.
In the Eurogamer Control Resonant review, Alexis Ong felt the game's larger, more open world setting leaves behind the magic of the original Control.

item.description:
A lot has already been said of Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Switch 2 port. The game, with all its free DLC updates - including new monsters - will be available 5th December, arriving with local co-op support to harken back to those old Gathering Hall days on the PSP or 3DS (if you're an old-head, like me).
It's looking like an ambitious port - something that shouldn't be that surprising to anyone familiar with Capcom's other Switch 2 projects. Pragmata, Resident Evil Requiem and more have all been well-recieved, mostly thanks to the immense amount of technical work the developer's engineers put into the ports.
Now, in an interview with Kotaku, Capcom has shed a little bit more light on how it's managed to get a game as complicated and sizeable as Monster Hunter Wilds - that's had (in)famous performance complaints - running on the Switch 2. Turns out, it's been a "painstaking process".
"The Nintendo Switch 2 version of Monster Hunter Wilds was developed around the concept of delivering a natural Monster Hunter Wilds experience on Nintendo Switch 2," producer Genki Sunano told the publication. "In other words, we didn't want it to feel like a simple port, where the graphics or performance had merely been scaled down to make the game run on Nintendo Switch 2." Sunano went on to state that the company's goal was to bring the same experience people have had on PC or console to Nintendo Switch 2 "without compromising the experience of Monster Hunter Wilds".
But doing that was not easy. "It was this painstaking, and at times seemingly endless, process of making decisions and optimisations one by one that proved to be one of our biggest challenges in delivering a comfortable handheld experience while preserving what makes Wilds feel like Wilds." The result seems to be agreeable, at least: the game runs at a solid 30FPS in handheld mode, even when running taxing multiplayer hunts.
And this will all help lay the foundations for this version of the game - and others - as Capcom gets ready to deploy the massive new content update at some point in 2027. "We plan to apply the knowledge and expertise gained through this project to the performance improvements that we will be making for existing platforms in the lead-up to the release of Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance."
I'm curious to see how the final game runs on Switch 2: I like how it performs and looks on my PS5 Pro, and I'm wondering if I'll be able to trade in the lush visuals and buttery performance for the ease of slaying hundreds of Rathalos on the go. I'll be picking up a copy on Switch 2 either way, but the jury is out on where my 'home' for the game is going to be, come December.
We know that Capcom has been sinking a lot of time into Wilds, with the publisher's eventual goal orientated towards "surpassing" the dizzying heights of Monster Hunter World and its popularity. To this end, it seems Capcom has all hands on deck with the upcoming expansion, Ascendance, something we're hoping to see more of in due course.

item.title: Crimson Desert developer Pearl Abyss today announced it's delaying Charting the Unknown, the game's first post-launch add-on. Previously set for release 15th October, the DLC's release date has been pushed back to 29th October - a two-week delay. Read more
item.description:
Crimson Desert developer Pearl Abyss today announced it's delaying Charting the Unknown, the game's first post-launch add-on. Previously set for release 15th October, the DLC's release date has been pushed back to 29th October - a two-week delay.
"We are hard at work on Crimson Desert Enhanced: Charting the Unknown to bring you new adventures to Pywel. However, we have determined that we need additional development time to deliver a more polished and stable gameplay experience," the developer said in a note posted on X.
Charting the Unknown was surprisingly announced early last month during a Sony State of Play presentation. Although we'd known Pearl Abyss was working on some sort of add-on for some time, September's reveal was the first confirmation of it, and our first look at it.
Charting the Unknown brings new destinations to the continent of Pywel, chiefly allowing players to explore the ocean through ships and underwater adventures. The journey will take players to new islands off the coast of Pywel, where new stories featuring protagonists Kliff, Oongka, and Damiane will unfold.
The add-on also includes new features such as an upgraded house-building mechanic, the ability to manage and rent facilities to earn cash, and a system that lets you grow your bonds with NPCs.
"We know many of you have been looking forward to returning to the game and we sincerely apologise for the longer wait. We will use the additional time to further refine the content and do our utmost to deliver the best experience we can," the developer added.
Charting the Unknown is priced £19.99 / $24.99. It's available for all versions of the game, except for the Mac App Store version.

item.title: The rumoured Xbox Mythic Achievements - the equivalent of PlayStation's Platinum Trophies - have been officially announced, and they're rolling out for Xbox Insiders now. Read more
item.description:
The rumoured Xbox Mythic Achievements - the equivalent of PlayStation's Platinum Trophies - have been officially announced, and they're rolling out for Xbox Insiders now.
Microsoft announced Mythic Achievements yesterday evening and, as expected, they're awarded when you earn all the other Achievements for a game - exactly the requirements needed to earn a Platinum Trophy on PlayStation.
Mythics are not affected by Achievement-adding DLC (Achievements added after a game's release are labelled as "add-on" Achievements) and perhaps most importantly, they're awarded retroactively, as far back as for Xbox 360 games. That means you could have a fat pile of Mythics as soon as they're turned on, providing you've actually Achievement-completed lots of games, that is.
Mythics arrive as part of an Achievement tidy-up on Xbox, which brings with it a new Gaming tab for profiles that organises Achievement-hunting progress better. You can also browse friends' Gaming tabs if you're hoping to feel superior to them.
Mythics follow a string of incremental Xbox updates from this year - such as some slight rebranding and a player feedback forum - that have had to contend with what's been an otherwise incredibly turbulent year for Microsoft's gaming division. It started with longtime leader Phil Spencer leaving Xbox early in the year, and was followed by sweeping layoffs and restructuring as new leader Asha Sharma took over and sought to make business sense of what she inherited.
The most recent wave of Xbox restructuring occurred last week, with a further 268 layoffs, studio consolidation, and what looks to be the impending closure of Hellblade developer Ninja Theory.

item.title: After about a month in testing, Xbox's disc-to-digital feature has officially launched for all owners of Xbox consoles. The feature allows users to turn Xbox One and Xbox Series X discs into digital copies. Read more
item.description:
After about a month in testing, Xbox's disc-to-digital feature has officially launched for all owners of Xbox consoles. The feature allows users to turn Xbox One and Xbox Series X discs into digital copies.
Microsoft said disc-to-digital works with "most" physical games across the two Xbox generations, but that not all games are eligible. This criteria may also change over time due to "technical, licensing, publishing, manufacturing, and other factors", according to Xbox's official support page.
If you're unfamiliar, here's how disc-to-digital works: when you insert a compatible Xbox One or Xbox Series X disc into your console, you'll have the option to turn that game into a digital copy. Doing so ties the game to your account, removing the need for the disc to be inserted for authentication each time you want to play.
That digital license also moves with the disc, meaning the original owner can later sell or give away their copy. The disc's new owner can utilise the same process to receive their own digital copy, revoking the original owner's license. In other words, the feature theoretically offers the best of both digital and physical.
Games that support Xbox Play Anywhere will be available to download and play on PC through the Xbox app, too. An easy way to check supported games is to filter your library by Play Anywhere support and see which have the disc-to-digital badge.
The release version of the disc-to-digital feature also includes an option to prevent discs from automatically starting the installation process. This is useful when you're converting multiple discs in a row and only want the console to recognise the disc for digitisation without installing the game.
If you intend on digitising your collection, it's worth skimming through the disc-to-digital Xbox support page to familiarise yourself with error codes and other problems that may arise.

item.title: On top of featuring all the game modes you expect from a Call of Duty game, Modern Warfare 4 is courting the competitive scene with something entirely new for the series: a game mode called Collateral. Read more
item.description:
On top of featuring all the game modes you expect from a Call of Duty game, Modern Warfare 4 is courting the competitive scene with something entirely new for the series: a game mode called Collateral.
Collateral is a more restrictive take on the series' classic Search and Destroy mode, aligning its rules more closely with those of the Bomb Defusal mode in Counter-Strike and Valorant. Search and Destroy was already seen as Call of Duty's version of that, but Collateral looks to be a more authentic recreation that strips away typical COD mechanics.
Collateral operates on an in-game cash economy where pre-made loadouts are disabled, and all players start with the same amount of money and a pistol. Teams alternate between attacking and defending two bomb sites, earning cash each round to spend on a standard set of weapons and equipment.
Just like in Counter-Strike, weapons and equipment are lost on death, but earned cash is kept. Collateral also disables automatic health regeneration, respawning and Killstreaks - except for the UAV, which is only available as a team buy and not for individual purchase. Perks are available, but they're limited and must also be acquired using cash, forcing players to make tough choices.
The list of what you can spend cash on should feel familiar to anyone who played a Counter-Strike game before. You'll also notice a lot of non-descript weapons designed to fill certain roles. Here's what you can purchase between rounds in Collateral:
Collateral's announcement was strangely tucked away near the end of a blog post about the technology and features of Modern Warfare 4's PC version, though there's no indication the mode is exclusive to PC.
This latest reveal comes in a week where Activision has seemingly been saying all the right things to entice lapsed players to buy Modern Warfare 4. The company announced a silly skin off toggle for Warzone, and is finally changing double XP tokens so they count down in match and not in real-time.
Modern Warfare 4 is set for release on 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.title: The Witcher 3's newly released Remastered edition has dramatically rekindled interest in the 11-year-old role-playing game, which is currently enjoying its highest concurrent player-count on Steam ever. Read more
item.description:
The Witcher 3's newly released Remastered edition has dramatically rekindled interest in the 11-year-old role-playing game, which is currently enjoying its highest concurrent player-count on Steam ever.
As of the time of writing, nearly 120,000 people are playing The Witcher 3 on Steam, making it the ninth most-played game on the PC platform. That of course does not include numbers from the likes of GOG and the Epic Games Store, where it's also being sold, nor the players on PlayStation, Switch 2, and Xbox.
According to Steam data-tracking website SteamDB, that's the highest concurrent player-count The Witcher 3 has ever had - higher than at its launch in 2015 (a high of 92K), and higher than the game's previous peak of 103K in January 2020, when Netflix's Witcher show was at its most popular. The other notable peak was 89K in December 2022, when the next-gen update dropped.
With a playerbase of 65 million, there's a large community to excite, but it's a reminder of how much pulling-power CD Projekt Red's fantasy RPG has, all the same. And as America wakes up and downloads the update, the question is how high can the numbers go?
The Remastered edition of the Witcher 3 rolls out today, bringing with it a vast array of upgrades to the way it looks and plays. Though as I found out while playing The Witcher 3 - Remastered, the changes aren't as quite as transformative as some might hope, and it's still very much the same game.
Nevertheless, this Remastered update being free to owners of any version of The Witcher 3 - and the game's existing expansions Hearts of Stone and Blood of Wine being thrown in for free as well - represents extraordinary game-support and generosity on the part of CD Projekt Red. And it's being done to prime the audience for the arrival of the new Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past next year.

The outrageously enjoyable Hades musical orchestral concert, Ballads of the Underworld, is now available to watch in its entirety, online, for free.
You might recall that Hades show being one we wrote about during Eurogamer's Optimism Week, in an article about our love of game-music performances. You remembered correctly: in that article we mentioned a few shows but the Hades performance was really the spark for it.
In the show, game-maker Supergiant recreated music from the Hades series with a live orchestra - the London Mozart Players - conducted by Hades co-composer Austin Wintory. There was also live singing from Melinoë actor Judy Alice Lee, Erin Yvette (Scylla), and Colin Ryan (Apollo). Supergiant composer Darren Korb and vocalist Ashley Barret also sung their hearts out.
The video is segmented according to a setlist listed in the video's description. My personal highlights are Moonlight Guide Us at the top of the show (it's a pity the encore version didn't make it in; they had another go at it); I am Gonna Claw (Out Your Eyes Then Drown You to Death) at 16.48; Colin Ryan singing Fated Glory at 46.00 (that voice!); and Darren Korb's incredible falsetto during the final few numbers. Great show, great games, great voices!
Also in Supergiant news, game documentary maker Noclip has released the first episode in its new series focusing on the development of Hades 2. Supergiant itself is currently working out what comes next after Hades 2. Nothing has yet been announced.

item.title: If you've been playing Medieval vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker and you're wondering why you're having a hard time during the day, as a human, versus as at night as a vampire, then don't worry: you're experiencing the game as intended. item.description:
If you've been playing Medieval vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker and you're wondering why you're having a hard time during the day, as a human, versus as at night as a vampire, then don't worry: you're experiencing the game as intended. It's not supposed to be balanced, apparently.
"Yes, you should," game director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz told me when I asked if you should feel more powerful as a vampire, and more underpowered as a human. "You should. When I created the idea for the protagonist the Dawnwalker, it was supposed to be something like the werewolf, which in the day as a human [you are] weaker than at night.
"But it's possible to play and finish the game [as a human] and it makes you always more grounded, and it allows us to tell the stories with different antagonists or different events where you will not be overpowered, and you don't need - like in the superhero movies - to create even stronger villains every time you create a new story."
I experienced this disparity in power while playing The Blood of Dawnwalker for review. I specifically noted that where I didn't succeed in assaulting the vampire Brencis' castle in the day in human form, but instead succeeded at night as a vampire shortly after. Tomaszkiewicz unpacked a few of the reasons why the vampire form is more powerful a little later into our chat.
"The first of them is that your damage with the claws develops with your level, which means that you don't need to spend points anywhere," Tomazkiewicz said. "You can boost it in the character development but with every level, your claws are stronger. In human form, you need to find a better sword, buy it or upgrade it.
"The second thing is that to heal in combat in human form, you need to craft potions, because without them you cannot heal yourself while you are fighting. In vampire form, you can heal by biting your enemies, and you can also drink consumables like the blood vials that you find in the world. Additionally, you can develop your vampire skills so you have a lot more health, like another segment of [your health bar], and after combat, this segment will always regenerate to full. And you can, of course, drink the animals, humans, and so on to refill your blood."
One other thing is a skill you can unlock as a vampire that replaces health when you attack. "It means that the vampire has a lot more abilities which make him stronger than the human," he said. "And that was the idea to differentiate it like this."
The vampire form's power is balanced by protagonist Coen having access to witchcraft abilities through the day which aren't accessible at night, and these spells can be hugely powerful, though I found Coen's being a witch a bit narratively underexplored and confusing next to him also being a vampire. It felt more like this originated from a mechanical point of view.
That seems to tally somewhat with what Tomaszkiewicz said. "We knew that [day and night] needed to be different, but we also knew that they needed to be interesting because we were afraid that if, in the human form, you did not have some strong skills that allowed you to finish the game, it would be problematic from many points," he said.
This is where witchcraft came in. "But the special skills we created, we thought they needed to be maybe not equally [powerful], but they needed to be good," Tomaszkiewicz said. "Vampires should always be stronger, but as a human with witchcraft, you should also have strong skills for many reasons."
Also, perhaps you don't like being a vampire, he said - which seems like an odd preference if you're going to play a vampire RPG like this. Or maybe you want a human-specific ending, because, "In human form, you have a few ways you can finish the game," Tomasziewicz said. "I don't want to spoil it too much, but you can do it by yourself, maybe with the allies, and more," he teases. Maybe you merely want to mix things up - the game is all about 'freedom of choice' after all, therefore your approach should be up to you.
Still, at least it's official: the hardest way to finish The Blood of Dawnwalker is in human form.
The Blood of Dawnwalker was released at the beginning of September and seems to have been a success, selling 1m copies in three days, though no updated sales figures have been released since then. Solid reviews were tainted slightly by gripes about game performance, technical issues, and some gameplay quirks. But the good news in this regard is The Blood of Dawnwalker's first major patch may be only days away, with an update planned for early October.
The divisive time mechanic is not being patched out, though, much to some people's frustration, I'm sure, though I really liked it. But apparently this time mechanic was once much stricter in early designs of The Blood of Dawnwalker, and even though it features heavily in this game, the time mechanic won't necessarily return for future Blood of Dawnwalker games.

item.title: Early access to Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is now available to owners of the game's Deluxe Edition, but the launch has been soured due to publisher Bandai Namco's handling of one particular pre-order bonus. Read more
item.description:
Early access to Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is now available to owners of the game's Deluxe Edition, but the launch has been soured due to publisher Bandai Namco's handling of one particular pre-order bonus.
Pre-ordering any version of Ace Combat 8 comes with a copy of Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War, and longtime fans were especially looking forward to this re-release because this 2006 game never appeared on anything other than PlayStation 2.
PC players were led to believe their copy of The Belkan War would be a separate product, because this is the way it works on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Something changed on Steam, however, to make the game DLC for Ace Combat 8 instead. Should it remain this way, it presents a number of associated problems, such as having to download a huge modern game to access a comparatively tiny old game, and the inability to run The Belkan War separately on weaker hardware, such as the Steam Deck.
It's not what the game's Steam listing used to say. At some point, the description was changed from "Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War is a standalone application separate from the Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve full game" to: "Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War (Steam version) is available as a DLC executable launched separately from the base game. Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve must be installed in order to utilize DLCs."
It's not clear when the store page was updated to alter the wording of the pre-order bonus, but you can see this Reddit post from earlier this month where players wonder how The Belkan War was going to be accessible come launch.
In the post, a user who pre-ordered Ace Combat 8 on Steam was unable to find The Belkan War in their Steam library. The user attached a screenshot of the game's Steam page where it clearly shows the older version of the verbiage, hence their confusion.
That same quiet-change is referenced in many of Ace Combat 8's negative Steam reviews, and it's among the hottest topics on the Ace Combat subreddit at the moment, overshadowing discussions about the game itself.
Making The Belkan War an add-on rather than standalone has significant drawbacks. For one, you need to download and install the full game of AC8 - ~135GB - in order to play a port of a 2006 game that is itself under 4GB.
As one Reddit user noted, this also prevents The Belkan War from being easily playable on Steam Deck. "I had no hope of AC8 running on my Steam Deck," the user wrote. "I preordered it on Steam specifically to play Zero on Deck. Because we were promised a standalone app."
Ace Combat 8 is significantly more demanding on Steam Deck hardware, but a re-release of a 20-year-old game isn't likely to be. Being nested under a different game also means The Belkan War doesn't have its own achievements, nor support cloud saves. Play time, captured screenshots and all other profile-related items must now also exist under the umbrella game.
Given that The Belkan War has its own install folder within Ace Combat 8's directory, it can technically be launched separately by locating its .exe file, but the main game needs to be installed regardless. This is especially frustrating as none of these issues exist on consoles, where the game is a standalone app with all that entails.
At the time of writing, Ace Combat 8 has a Mixed user review rating on Steam, based on over 1,350 reviews. It will be interesting to see if that changes when the official 2nd October release date arrives.

item.title: Another country has entered the fray as ongoing debates around digital video game ownership ignite across the world. Read more
item.description:
Another country has entered the fray as ongoing debates around digital video game ownership ignite across the world.
President of the Mexican Senate’s Digital Rights Commission, Luis Donaldo Colosio Riojas, has revealed a new initiative via his personal Instagram account that he - alongside federal deputy Iraís Reyes - were proposing changes to legislation that would better protect consumers in Mexico in an increasingly digital consumer landscape.
The main points of this initiative are geared towards providing better clarity on what people are actually buying when they purchase a digital product, which would force companies to clarify whether people are actually buying a product or just a licence to use said product.
It also pushes for some manner of digital preservation after servers are taken down, allowing those who purchase digital goods to continue playing some form of a game after they are no longer officially supported. This aligns with similar goals seen in Californian consumer rights arguments from earlier this year.
Finally - and perhaps most importantly for Mexican gaming enthusiasts - the pair are pushing for additional accountability for companies that sell digital goods in Mexico. At the moment, many of these companies do not have consumer-facing support in Mexico, and this proposition aims to change that by forcing businesses to have a Mexican business address so authorities can intervene if consumer rights issues occur.
This push from Colosio and Reyes comes at a time when the shift towards a fully digital gaming landscape is becoming more likely. With Sony planning to end physical disc support in 2028, groups like Stop Killing Games have put pressure on the EU to introduce greater consumer rights protections. Colosio and Reyes filed an antitrust complaint against Sony following its announced shift away from physical games earlier this year.
The shift to digital has proven controversial, with many enthusiasts expressing their displeasure towards Sony following its announcement. Last week, Sony reportedly polled game developers about their feelings about the shift to digital, indicating perhaps this planned move to a digital-only future may yet be up in the air.

item.description:
Xbox and The Coalition are making a big deal about Gears of War: E-Day's campaign, ahead of its Xbox and PC launch on 1st October. The game goes back in time to study the origins of the Locust scourge, placing you in the big, stompy shoes of a younger and more 'innocent' Marcus Fenix as he navigates the beginning of the end of the world with erstwhile comrade, Dom Santiago. As I noted in my preview, it feels like a continuation of the original trilogy - somehow! - in its pacing, mechanics, and setup.
But one thing I remained curious about was how far The Coalition might push its difficulty. Gears, as a series, is infamous for being a tough shooter that relies on taking advantage of cover and weapon variety in order to progress. Traditionally, completing the game on the hardest Insane difficulty has been something of a badge of honour for players - similar to how nailing a LASO (Legendary, all skulls on) in Halo games was an achievement worthy of celebration.
So, does E-Day honour that legacy? "Luckily for us, we worked a lot on the various difficulty modes in Gears 4 and Gears 5, so I think we were able to follow a lot of those same patterns," says Matt Searcy, creative director at The Coalition, when I ask him about balancing difficulty for fun and challenge.
"Because of the Gears formula - which is the layout of the spaces, the weapons you're given, and the enemy combinations we put together - when you turn the difficulty dial up in Gears, the puzzle emerges more. I think that's one of the things that makes Gears really cool, right? That makes you, as a player, think. It's not just 'How fast can I Whack-a-Mole?' or 'Can I find the strongest weapon?' It's more 'What is the best strategy?' And [the puzzle] also changes if you're in co-op or if you're a single player."
Searcy goes on to say that The Coalition, essentially, breaks down the pillars of the Gears experience to its constituent parts in order to put it back together and assemble a campaign that is challenging, but fair. "If we build great spaces, good enemy combinations, and invest a lot more in the Locust and what they can do, then the difficulty balancing does take some time, but a lot of good comes out of it.
"And a kind of cool thing about Gears as well, I think, is that it's very inviting to play how you want to play. You want to crank the difficulty? You want to play Hardcore? You want to play co-op, but you want it harder than your friends? We allow that; we have split difficulty. So if you want to play on Insane and your buddy isn't as good as you, they can play on Normal and you can go through it together because everything is balanced off of [individual] damage and health. This is a really special thing for the franchise, I think."
So, given that there are four difficulty modes in the Campaign - Casual, Normal, Hardcore, Insane - is there an intended difficulty for the overall experience? "Yeah, I can tell you right now," laughs Searcy when I ask. "It's Hardcore. So, the game defaults to Normal, but we play it on Hardcore. If you think about the world, brutality is one of our pillars. And like, Gears of War is meant to be a hard thing. The violence there is like a cathartic release, and when you chainsaw and you hear the character go 'fuck yeah!' we want you to be feeling that way too - because the way you got there should have been difficult and hard. And Hardcore is the best way for experiencing that. All the mechanics are firing kind of at the top of their game, but if you stick your head out of cover or make the wrong decision, you get knocked on your ass."
By including a variety of mechanics - including 'down but not out' opportunities, limited to two per encounter - The Coalition demonstrates that it understands the push-and-pull necessary to make a difficult game fun: you need to be punished for taking risks that are slightly too egregious, but at the same time, you need to be rewarded for pushing back against the tide that is perpetually threatening to overwhelm you.
I note how much I enjoyed the 'invisible hand' of the developer guiding me during some tricky sections of the preview: you spawn in behind a car when you meet your first 'Boomer' (read: an oversized Locust with a one-hit-kill grenade launcher), and I charged him head-on only to end up as a wet pool of chunky meat on the floor.
"Did you think 'Maybe I should go get behind that car over there?'" laughs Searcy. "Or 'Maybe I should have stayed behind the car the devs put me behind in that cutscene' [laughter]. You say 'invisible hand', but I think occasionally in our game it's more that our hand is there, smacking you on your ass, saying 'Get back in cover'!"
I enjoyed my preview of Gears of War: E-Day. It felt transportative, taking me back to many a misspent evening as a teenager, trying to complete Insane playthroughs in Gears 1 through 3 with an old friend, banging my head against the brutality and grinding difficulty of those three Epic-made campaigns. If the full game can live up to that sense of tension and achievement with its balance, then - for my money - The Coalition will have made a very successful prequel to one of gaming's most infamous trilogies.

item.description:
Why did The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim never receive a spin-off like Bethesda's Fallout 3 did, with Fallout: New Vegas? According to Skyrim co-lead designer Kurt Kuhlmann, it's because of The Elder Scrolls Online. Speaking to FRVR (via VGC), the 20-year studio veteran said the MMORPG essentially kept Elder Scrolls fans occupied while Bethesda focused on other projects.
"I do think The Elder Scrolls Online took the heat off," Kuhlmann said. "There was a new Elder Scrolls product, and it was ongoing. It was creating new content constantly."
Kuhlmann explained that although the series had always been known as a single-player experience, The Elder Scrolls Online changed that, and ended up being the main ESO game for a lot of players.
"There are a lot of people… I mean, I know [there are] the single-player people, I'm one of those people - but there are a lot of people to whom The Elder Scrolls is now The Elder Scrolls Online. That's their experience with it. That's what they love. That's where they got their Elder Scrolls gaming experience, and that's probably what they want more of."
Another reason why Skyrim never got its own New Vegas spin-off has to do with that game's popularity and critical acclaim, which started something of a rivalry between Bethesda and New Vegas developer Obsidian.
"The whole New Vegas thing did create this - at least the perception of this - 'Who makes a better Fallout game? Oh, they should just give it to Obsidian' [situation]," Kuhlmann pointed out.
"There are the Obsidian, New Vegas people that think obviously New Vegas is way better, Obsidian is way better at making those games, and why don't they just get Fallout altogether," he went on.
By Kuhlmann's assessment, series creator Todd Howard didn't want a repeat of that situation within The Elder Scrolls series. "Todd, from my time there, he is very protective of it," he added.
Obsidian, of course, was recently confirmed to have started working on a new Fallout game in collaboration with Bethesda, following sweeping cuts across the Xbox division. Last week, another round of reorganisation moved Obsidian fully under Bethesda's purview.
As for The Elder Scrolls Online, the game's development will continue, but severe cuts at its studio Zenimax Online mean the scope of future additions has changed, even as Zenimax Online continues to reassure fans that ESO is not going away.
The Elder Scrolls 6 remains in development, with Bethesda claiming the layoffs have not affected its development roadmap. The game has no public release target.
